en: In the Tang dynasty, there was a Great Being named Daoxuan, whose courtesy name was Fabian. Gifted with divine intuition from Heaven, he penetrated deeply into the very marrow of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
He reached a definitive understanding that the Vinaya is itself the Perfect Vehicle (*paripūrṇayāna*).

He himself composed various works, including the *Jieshu*, the *Jiemoshu*, and the *Xingshi chao*; through these, the study of the Vinaya was widely disseminated throughout the world. It is said that from—
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, this master alone was the one who promoted and established the Vinaya in the world.
Subsequently, there were no fewer than sixty or more eminent monks and sages of our school who recorded his teachings;
nevertheless, because the patriarch’s compositions were concise and archaic, and their underlying meanings were profound and subtle, many of these later schools lost the true intent.

The Patriarch’s intent was fully realized by the Great Master Dazhi of the Song dynasty, who, at an early age, possessed such brilliant insight that he applied himself with keen resolve to the Vinaya.

He thoroughly investigated the textual principles and attained a profound understanding of the Patriarch’s intent. Consequently, he composed various commentaries, including the *Xingzong ji*, the *Jiyuan ji*, and the *Zichi ji*, which comprehensively explain the texts of that school.
Those who recognize his work consider it to surpass the interpretations of more than sixty other masters. — Yuan [Dynasty] Record.
In the third month of spring in the *ruò rén wǔ* year, a certain person of the Zǐ clan came to present a copy of the *Xíngshìchāo*, the *Zīchíjì Xùjiě*, and a single volume of the *Wǔlì Jiǎngyì*.
He earnestly requested that I proofread them for circulation within our own country, to which I joyfully agreed.
Upon opening and reading them quickly, I found they were the works of Tà'ān Lǜ, a high-ranking disciple of the Great Wisdom Master (Dàzhì).
This was compiled by the Master. According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Sengzhuan*), his family name, given name, and native place are not detailed;

however, it is recorded that he authored this work, as well as the preface and commentary to the *Suiji jiemó* (Karmavācanā according to Circumstances), all of which have circulated widely throughout the world.

Observing how he clarified the defense against insults and the remediation of defects, and how he brought forth the essential tenets, it is evident that he did not merely investigate the Vinaya studies, but extensively traversed the Tripitaka and the classics of the nine schools of thought. Furthermore...
The contribution to our school has been truly great. Less than ten days after it was completed, the proofreading was finalized;
I have therefore entrusted it to the woodblock carvers to have it engraved. Written with devotion by the śramaṇa Śīlacandra Guānguāng of Tángzhāotí Temple in Nánjīng, at the Yìngliàng Fāng.
Preface to the *Commentary on the Essentials for the Practice of the Vinaya* (Xing-shi-chao Zi-chi-ji) and Exegesis of the Five Examples, by the Disciple Ze’an.

In the title, the first six characters indicate that which is explained (*so-jie*), while the final three characters indicate that which explains (*neng-jie*). Within that which explains, the first two characters [indicate... [Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a traditional Chinese Buddhist preface and commentary. The translation reflects the structure and terminology of the original.]

The title of the *Commentary* (*shu*) pertains to the specific [text], as it differs from ancient times; the following single character [of the title] pertains to the general, as it is common to all records.

Furthermore, the title of the *Sub-commentary* (*chao*) pertains to the general, as it provides a comprehensive explanation for over fifty schools; the title of the *Record* (*ji*) pertains to the specific, as the designation "Zizhi" (Supporting the Practice) is restricted to our own school.

Moreover, the name established for the title of the *Sub-commentary* is based upon ritual practice; reflecting back upon the models of the nine generations, it serves as a guide for those currently receiving the benefits of this tradition.
Within the teachings, there is nothing that transcends these two characters, "intent" (yì) and "practice" (xíng). These appear throughout various texts:

the *Jiàoxù* states, "To manifest practice in worldly affairs" and "sharply harboring the intent for practice"; the commentary on the *Jièxù* states, "As for practice, one frequently encounters hesitation";

the preface to the *Yèshū* states, "As for practice, its ultimate destination has not yet been seen"; and the *Qīngzhòng yí* states, "The practices of the various masters are based on their realization."
The Preface to the *Platform Sūtra* states: "The Vinaya is the broad essentials; its practice is the plan.

Thus we know that the practice of the Vinaya is the root source of the Buddha's transformation of beings and the very core of the teachings' true meaning. Although various masters have composed treatises, they have never taken this into account.
What this present compendium elucidates returns entirely to the practice of the Vinaya. As Confucius said: "To entrust [truth] to empty words is not as good as embodying it in actual practice."

This is profoundly clear and manifest. Because the Master of the Record deeply embodied the intent of the teachings, he established this auspicious title. His preface states: "Looking up to the principles of ritual practice, it is titled *Zichi* (Supporting and Sustaining).

"Supporting" (*zi*) refers to the various practices performed by the community both individually and collectively; "sustaining" (*chi*) refers to the two types of observance: abstention and performance.

While there are differences in how these three practices and two observances are categorized and combined, the preface further states: "The entire treatise is unified within the three practices, and the three practices do not transcend the two."

The *Chiyi chao* (Notes on the Meaning of Holding) states: "The two 'holdings' (*chi*) are arrayed in rows, yet they both return to the three practices. From this, one knows that the title *Zichi* (Aiding and Holding) is precisely the title of the *Chao* (Commentary);
although the names for the practice and the subject differ, their meaning is in fact no different. The capacity and the object correspond perfectly, like a box and its lid.

"Aiding" (*zi*) takes the sense of assisting and eliciting; "holding" (*chi*) is the name manifested in contrast to transgressions. Although the aspects of holding are many, they are essentially divided into two.

The "observance through performance" (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*) is established with respect to wholesome matters, while the "observance through restraint" (*vārita-dhāraṇa*) is established with respect to unwholesome matters.

Since no objective circumstance transcends the categories of wholesome and unwholesome, these two observances are distinguished based on this duality of wholesome and unwholesome. Thus, there is not a single matter that is not a locus for upholding the precepts;
"upholding" means protecting what was originally received in accordance with one's conduct. The *Chao* (Excerpts) states: "There is restraint, yet there is no..."

To violate the luminous purity of the precept-essence and to accord with what was originally received is termed "observance" (*dhāraṇā*). Although various schools clarify two types of offenses, their intent lies in establishing two forms of observance;
thus, we know that the practice of observance is truly the core of the teaching. To abandon the practice of observance is insufficient for discussing the Vinaya.

Therefore, the teaching arises to accommodate the capacities of sentient beings, and observance is manifested through the teaching. Now, as for the "observance" (*dhāraṇā*) that relies upon the expressive teaching:

That which is expounded is practice; because the teaching assists practice, it is called "Support" (*zizhi*). This is like Tiantai’s *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) or Huayan’s *Zhuoxiu* (Aids to Cultivation).

As stated below: "In analyzing and explaining the words and phrases, one values profound clarity regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), weighing their practical applications so that one may fully uphold and follow [the teachings].
Thus, by raising the title once, both teaching and practice are propagated together, benefiting both oneself and others.
The intent of the various schools is fully revealed here; one should know that this title originally derives from the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), which states:
"The five assemblies rely upon and uphold the perfected virtues through their resources. Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "That which is sustained by pure white dharmas.

Yet, the titles established by various masters all fail to grasp the purport of the *Chao* (Sub-commentary). Some establish names based on interpretations, while others designate titles according to locations. Since the names themselves are incorrect, what else need be said?
The *Zhuanhao* (Collection of Titles) and the *Zhuangshishu Wen* (Text on the Adornment of the Śākyas) state: "The present Houyang County in Liangguo is precisely the Shangqiu of Yebó.

[Gaoxinsi had two sons; the elder was named] Yebó. Weizi was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Song for over twenty generations, and it was from this that our Imperial House received its fief from the Zhou dynasty and subsequently rose like a dragon.
Therefore, it was taken as the title for possessing the empire. The *Tujing* (Atlas of Classics) states that it is Yuhang.

The county was established during the Qin dynasty and belonged to Kuaiji. It is said that "Yuhang" (Excess Boats) originated because when the First Emperor of Qin came to tour Kuaiji, he disembarked his ships here to travel by land;
thus it was named Yuhang. The Han dynasty retained this name, though Wang Mang changed it to Jinlu (Advance Land);
the Later Han restored the original name, and it subsequently became subordinate to Wujun. Other details are as recorded in the *Zidaoji* (Record of the Way of Resources).

"Śramaṇa" is a term from the Sanskrit language; here it is translated as "diligent in cessation. This means being diligent in performing various good deeds and ceasing all evils. The *Huashou jing* (Sutra of the Flower-Head) says:
"Just as space is without contact or obstruction, and smoke and clouds have no place to travel, so too I say that the dharma of the śramaṇa is without defilement."

The commentary on "Śākya" states: King Śākyaśīvidha banished his four sons. When they first arrived at the Śākyavana forest north of the Snowy Mountains, the people there took refuge in them, and it developed into a powerful kingdom.
Later, when the king went to summon them, they declined and did not return.

From afar, he sighed and said, "My son is Śākya," which in the language of China means "Capable Benevolence" (Nengren). The Buddha is a descendant of that lineage; therefore, the fivefold assembly takes Śākya as their clan name.

Because those who have left the household life are disciples of the Buddha, they are generally addressed by [the master's surname]. Before the Jin and Wei dynasties, all followed the surname of their teacher;

for example, Master Zhigong had the surname Guan, but because his teacher was Zhi Falin, he was called Zhi Dun. Master Sheng had the surname Wei, but because his teacher was Zhu Fatai, he was called Zhu Daosheng.
Master Dao’an, however, said: "Once one has shaved one’s hair and donned the dyed robes, one inherits the lineage of Śākyamuni; thus, there is no difference."
It is said that their surnames should all be Śākya; although this teaching exists, it may not yet have been fully realized. However, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states regarding the fruits [of the path]:

"The four rivers enter the sea and no longer retain their original names; so too do those of the four castes who leave the household life all equally call themselves sons of the Śākyas. Furthermore, the *Mahīśāsaka Vinaya* says:
"You who have left the household life from various backgrounds all abandon your original surnames and equally call yourselves sons of the Śākyas."
"Compilation" (zhuàn) refers to taking up the brush and pen to arrange phrases into chapters;

the general outline of this preface consists of praising the fundamental essence, distinguishing the source of the teachings, narrating the wide propagation, and extending the intent of the author's composition. By examining the preface, one may recognize its origins and purpose.

In the first section, the praise of the essence of the school, there are three parts. First, the initial phrase identifies the person who received [the teaching]; second, the following six phrases constitute the actual praise, which is further divided into two:
the first two phrases describe the practice of the school, and the subsequent lines clarify its function; finally, "sincerity" serves as the concluding summary.

Regarding those who first leave the household life, there are two types of karmic dispositions as described in the *Yebao cunzhai jing shu* (Commentary on the Sūtra of the Merit of the Eight Precepts):

First, those who leave other households with the resolve to seek liberation and forever distance themselves from entanglements and fetters; this is the fundamental type. As stated in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, one who leaves home not for the sake of liberation cannot be called a *saṃgha*.

Second, those who possess the capacity for great benefit and whose minds long to transcend the secular world; although their physical form remains in the secular realm, their nature is fundamentally constant and firm, never wavering.
Regarding the statement "purity through verbal restriction," it says: "You need only resolve your mind, and you are a renunciant. This can be analyzed into four propositions: 1.

Having already renounced the world, one follows the Way with the intent to seek liberation; this is the case where both body and mind have renounced. 2. Although the body is attached to the Way, the mind sinks into the secular world;

this is the case where the body has renounced but the mind has not. This refers to those who, weary of the hardships of domestic pursuits and seeking the life of a renunciant to escape them, yet still provide for their families.
"Joy is itself Nirvana. Regarding those who leave the home-life for the sake of food and clothing, there are three types as explained in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:

first, those whose minds have left the home-life while their bodies remain; second, those who are mired in and attached to the five desires, remaining bound to the household life; and third, those who have neither left the home-life [in mind nor in body]. What is meant here by "leaving the home-life" refers to the first of these.
The term "shi" (士) is a designation for one who possesses the Way (*mārga*), equivalent to what is commonly called a "gentleman" (*yiguan zhi shi*) in secular parlance.

Those who possess the Way and righteousness—these śramaṇas of this land fundamentally speak of the Path; they call a bodhisattva a "Great Being" (Mahāsattva) and a Buddha a "Supreme Being" (Anuttarapuruṣa).
Confucius said: "He who acts with a sense of shame, and when sent on an embassy to the four quarters does not disgrace his sovereign's mandate, may be called a 'gentleman' (Shi)."

In the initial passage of the "Correct Praise" (*Zhèngtàn*), the statement that "receiving the precepts constitutes the essence" means that receiving [the precepts] is the mind that takes them up as its object, while the precepts are the karma produced thereby.

The *Yèshū* (Commentary on Karma) states: "Karma is the essence of the precepts, because for those who have left the household life, there is no separate essence; rather, it is formed by grasping the Dharma. The *Jìlùn* (Treatise on Wisdom) says:
"Shaving the head and donning dyed robes constitute its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); upholding the prohibitive precepts constitutes its nature (*svabhāva*). This nature is precisely the essence.
Regarding "gathering the dharmas within one's person": "dharmas" refers to the dharmadhātu, the sands of the Ganges, the two truths, and so forth.
Speaking in terms of what has been realized within oneself, these are the "holy dharmas" (*āryadharma*). However, these various dharmas are currently scattered throughout the sensory environment;

now, by universally taking them as objects through a single thought-moment and gathering them back into the mind-consciousness, they fill the primary retribution (*upapatti*) to form a "collection of wholesome dharmas. The *Cao* (Commentary) states: "The monastics who have left the household life are truly wholesome."
The accumulation of the merits of the Dharma and the exalted status among humans and devas are both fundamentally due to this.

Next, the exposition of its function has two parts: first, describing the cultivation of causal practices based on the essential substance; second, describing the attainment of resultant virtues by conforming to the Dharma.

Furthermore, within the first part, there are two sections: first, taking the reception of the precepts as the substance; second, taking the accumulation of dharmas as residing in the person. Regarding those who cultivate based on the substance:

This refers to the skillful cultivation and purification [of the precepts]. The *Chao* (Excerpts) states: "Regarding 'conformity' (*anuvartana*), it means that after receiving the precepts, the mind that guards them in relation to their objects is successfully perfected through skillful means, corresponding to the original pure karma.

The *Jingye Shu* (Commentary on Pure Karma) clarifies that there are four types of conformity: first, the conformity of diligent non-transgression; second, the conformity of being able to repent after transgressing;
third, the conformity of guarding and maintaining [the precepts] without [deliberate] intent; and fourth, the conformity of being able to transgress without regret. Now...
What is clarified here refers solely to the preceding two [stages] in relation to the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of subsequent dharmas; thus, they are designated as "causes.
To act in accordance with the Dharma means that one's movements—whether walking or standing, or any other deportment (*īryāpatha*)—must necessarily follow the correct path. As the *Analects* states:

"Do not look at what is contrary to propriety (*li*), do not listen to what is contrary to propriety, do not speak what is contrary to propriety, and do not move in a manner contrary to propriety. It is appropriate, therefore, to be cautious and not to tread recklessly; only then can the three trainings (*triśikṣā*) and the eight... [be perfected].

It is precisely from this that the four wisdoms and three bodies arise, and it is by means of this that they are established; therefore, it is called the Dharmakāya. The *Saccaka-nigaṇṭhaputta Sūtra* states:
"The Tathāgata’s body, adorned with merits, takes the reception of the precepts as its essence and original observance of the precepts as its beginning.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "If one wishes to see the Buddha-nature and realize great nirvāṇa, one must cultivate and maintain purity with a profound mind."

The precepts all carry this meaning. The *dharmakāya* is constituted by the five factors: the three—precept (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*)—derive their names from the cause;

the two—liberation (*vimukti*) and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśana*)—manifest their titles from the fruit. Because one cuts off delusions through wisdom, the state where delusions no longer exist is called "liberation.

To emerge from the entanglements, break through obstructions, and reflect back to contemplate the mind is called "knowledge and vision of liberation. This is as stated in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*.
Regarding the three [liberations], one interpretation states: the first three are dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa), while the latter two are dharmas of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).

A second interpretation states that all are, within the stage of no-more-learning, wisdom (prajñā) consisting of resolute confidence (adhimokṣa); this is called the aggregate of liberation (vimukti-skandha). Wisdom regarding the truth of the path (mārga-satya) is called the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha), while wisdom regarding the other three truths is called the aggregate of wisdom (prajñā-skandha).
A third interpretation states that all are common to both those in training and those beyond training. If this is so, how are they distinguished?
Answer: One who is in the stage of training (śaikṣa) attains partial realization, whereas one in the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa) attains perfection.

Furthermore, the Great Teaching defines the Dharmakāya as being eternally blissful, self, and pure, forever free from all aging, illness, death, and so forth. However, there are two types of Dharmakāya: first, the Dharmakāya of Original Nature;
second, the Dharmakāya of Cultivated Attainment, also known as the two bodies of Principle and Phenomenon (*li-shi*). As clarified above, this refers to the Dharmakāya of Cultivated Attainment.

Although the natures of these [three bodies] differ in their cultivation, that which they manifest is without distinction. The *Yebushu* (Commentary on the *Yogācārabhūmi*) clearly explains the three bodies, namely: the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

The present text briefly cites them because it must respond to the preceding phrase; thus, it singles out the Dharma-body alone. Although its manifestation as transformation is not explicitly shown here, the principle necessarily entails the Reward-body.
This is what is meant by "whichever one body is cited, the three bodies are fully present. Furthermore, the Dharma-body is capable of manifesting transformation.

The "retribution" (*vipāka*) is discussed here based on the primary text. Alternatively, one may correlate the four lines as follows: the first line refers to the essence of the precept (*śīla-svabhāva*);

the second line, to the dharma of the precept (*śīla-dharma*); the lines below "conduct" (*caryā*), to the practice of the precept (*śīla-caryā*); and the lines above "body" (*kāya*), to the characteristics of the precept (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*). The first three [categories] are easily understood. Regarding the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there are two types:

first, the characteristic of the dharma (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), and second, the characteristic of conduct (*caryā-lakṣaṇa*). The thesis states: "When majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*) and conduct are perfected, whatever actions are performed, every movement must accord with the Dharma."

"Virtue is manifest" refers to the characteristics of clear conduct. The commentary on the characteristics states: "That which is clarified here extends throughout the *pāyattika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses;

this is the discernment of characteristics according to the Dharma. The text says: "Acting in accordance with the Dharma precisely accords with the established principle; this is the characteristic of practice (*caryā-lakṣaṇa*). Question: In the *Shu-chao*, the Dharma is presented first and the essence (*tǐ*) follows;
why is it that in the present text, the essence is presented first and the Dharma follows? Answer: The composition of the treatises varies according to the occasion; there is no fixed rule.

This is certainly so; moreover, the correlation of the four practices originates from the records of later worthies. Since the master of the records’ systematic exposition of his single period of teaching accords perfectly with the Dharma, commentators need not trouble themselves to alter or differ from the text when lecturing.

In the summary: there is no practice without substance, and no cultivation of the person without the Dharma. Since the perfection of conduct and the fullness of virtue must necessarily arise from pure precepts, it is said that they truly depend upon them.
Regarding "setting out toward the primary goal" (*faqu youzong*): "setting out" (*fa*) refers to initiating practice, while "toward" (*qu*) refers to what is aimed for;

"primary goal" (*zong*) specifically refers to the precepts. As the *Jiechao* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "Among the myriad practices of setting out, the precepts are the sovereign lord. "Relying" (*yi*) means obtaining a basis through causes and conditions; "basis" (*suoyi*) refers to that upon which one relies.
Because it relies upon and takes as its support meditative concentration and wisdom, the "cause" refers to the causal basis—namely, that which arises from concentration and wisdom;
the "place" likewise refers to the precepts. As the *Śāsanāpadeśa* states: "By relying on and depending upon these precepts, one gives rise to meditative concentration."
Next, regarding the section on the Tathāgata’s establishment of the Vinaya, the first part consists of two lines which clarify that the mind is fundamentally one true reality.

From below, this shows how delusion gives rise to the three paths. Within this, "one consciousness" refers to what the Patriarch said: "Do not falsely engage with objects; there is only the single consciousness. He also said:

"It returns to permeate the deluded mind within the fundamental storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). This points directly to the essence of the mind being the principle of Mahāyāna; such is its substance.
Pure and wondrous function, empty and pervasive, it encompasses the ten directions and nurtures all existence. In accordance with the needs of beings, it manifests in various forms:

the Dharma-realm, Nirvana, the Middle Way, the True Mark (dharmatā), Perfect Enlightenment, Prajñā, Suchness, True Emptiness, the Nature of Dharmas, Buddha-nature, Mind-only, Consciousness-only, the Buddha-treasury, the Buddha-mother, the Śūraṃgama-dhāraṇī, and so forth; it is also titled the Tathāgata.
The *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*, the *Samatā-viśuddhi-bodhi-sūtra*, and other scriptures state that Prajñā is a single dharma which the Buddha has taught under various names.
Now, relying upon the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, we shall clarify the ālayavijñāna.
In Sanskrit it is called *ālaya* or *āliya*; here it is translated as the "storehouse consciousness" (*zàngshí*). It contains and stores all causes and effects of both good and evil.
Regarding the seeds of defilement and purity, the *Awakening of Faith* states that True Suchness (*tathatā*) follows conditions (*pratyaya-anuvartana*) while being neither born nor extinguished;

its union with the arising-and-ceasing [consciousness], being neither identical nor different, is called the *ālayavijñāna*, which is subsumed under the consciousness of the union of the real and the false.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that external objects fundamentally do not exist as realities, and that "only consciousness exists" (*vijñaptimātra*) is the practice for realizing the Great Bodhi, the fruit of Buddhahood; this refers entirely to True Suchness.

According to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, there is a true consciousness that understands the profound mystery (saṃdhinirmocana), which speaks of nine consciousnesses. This refers to establishing a ninth, pure, true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*) distinct from the eighth consciousness;
it is also called the "pure and undefiled consciousness" or the "eternally pure and true consciousness. Now, based on the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, I shall briefly clarify three types of consciousness.
The sūtra states: "Briefly stated, there are three kinds of consciousness; extensively stated, there are eight kinds of characteristics. What are they?"

The third refers to the True Consciousness (which is True Suchness), the Manifesting Consciousness (also called the Storehouse Consciousness), and the Discriminating Consciousness of Phenomena (also called the Evolving Consciousness).

This is based on the principle that True Suchness, while conforming to conditions, remains unchanging and does not unite with delusion; thus it is the True Consciousness. When it remains unchanging yet conforms to conditions to arise in conjunction with them, it becomes the Manifesting Consciousness.
For example, it is like a bright mirror in which various forms and images appear. The remaining seven consciousnesses constitute the Discriminating Consciousness of Phenomena.
These three types [of consciousness] encompass all such explanations; that sutra also states:
"The Tathāgatagarbha is named the ālayavijñāna, which co-exists with ignorance and the seven consciousnesses, like the waves of a great ocean that are ever-present and uninterrupted.

Furthermore, because the Tathāgatagarbha is perfumed by beginningless false and evil habitual tendencies, it is called the *cittavijñāna* (store-consciousness). Now, it is clarified that the essence of this consciousness is fundamentally true.
Because it is pure, it is called "primordial luminosity" (*yuanming*). The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Thus, this essence of consciousness of yours is primordially luminous," and again:

"The nature of the ocean of awareness is tranquil and perfect; its perfect tranquility is primordial luminosity. This primordial luminosity shines forth and gives rise to the object; once the object is established, the nature of the shining light perishes.

However, this single consciousness has been equal for both Buddhas and sentient beings from the very beginning; since it cannot be found within the two conditions of defilement and purity, it is so called.
Defilement and purity are unobtainable.

To illustrate this within the state of delusion, the first two lines refer to the afflictions (*kleśa*): because this single consciousness does not maintain its own nature, it moves in response to objects;

this movement is the mark of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*). As this movement continues without ceasing, it blazes forth as the differentiation of sense-objects, manifesting transformations that create the world and sentient beings.

Regarding the distinctions among the ten realms—the lands, ordinary beings and sages, cause and effect, birth and Buddhahood, the environment and its inhabitants, and the primary and secondary—*The Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"Due to deluded ignorance there is empty space; based on space, worlds are established; when the appearances settle, they become lands; and conscious awareness constitutes sentient beings.

It further states: "Obscuration and darkness constitute emptiness; within this dark and obscured emptiness, darkness coagulates to form matter (*rūpa*); matter mingles with deluded thoughts, and these conceptualizations of appearances form the body. Furthermore:
The *Yeshu* (Commentary on Karma) states: "This is truly because sentient beings, from beginningless time, have been attached to the notions of 'this' and 'that,' 'gain' and 'loss.
It further states: "Transforming according to conditions, there arises 'that' and 'this'; therefore, it is said that 'self and other' burn fiercely. Below this, it clarifies the paths of karma:

"Contact" refers to moving in accordance with delusive objects; "arising" refers to the sudden emergence of delusive consciousness when encountering objects; and "feeling" refers to the mind being turned by those objects. Thus it is said.

Because the mind follows delusive objects and their characteristics merge, it is said that "karmic activity arises. The *Commentary on Karmic Activity* (*Ye shu*) states: "Following delusion, karmic activity arises; movement accords with delusion," and so forth.
The subsequent section concerns the path of suffering and those within the various realms of existence (*bhava*). The three realms are constricting like a prison. The *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"One is able to exert effort to deliver all sentient beings from the prison of the three realms. The *Commentary on Karmic Activity* states: "Due to this, defilement arises."

The "entanglements" (*paryavasthāna*) consist of the realms of existence (*bhava*). Since there are the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātu*) and the twenty-five realms of existence, they are called "all existences.

The myriad classes of beings refer to the six destinies and four modes of birth, which revolve and mutually undergo innumerable varieties of differentiation; hence, they are called "the myriad classes.

However, one should know that the ten realms—both the environment and its inhabitants, as well as the causes and effects of the six destinies—are all transformations of a single consciousness. Thus it should be understood.

Since there is not a single phenomenon that is not a transformation of consciousness within the single substance of consciousness, the Sūtra says: "In the three realms there are no distinct phenomena;
they are merely the creation of the one mind. It also says: "The three realms are mind-only; all phenomena are consciousness-only. Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states:
"I have always said that the conditions of form and mind, as well as the mental factors and all objects of cognition, are manifested solely by the mind."
It further states: "The physical body, mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth are all things within the wondrously luminous true mind;
it is only because of delusion and ignorance that one fails to realize this, thereby undergoing saṃsāra and remaining unable to transcend birth and death. It also states: "The Buddha told Ānanda:
'All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have followed various inverted karmic seeds; naturally, they are unable to achieve accomplishment.'"
Unsurpassed Bodhi arises entirely from not knowing two kinds of roots: first, the root of beginningless birth and death, which is this攀緣心 (攀緣心;
*pān-yuán-xīn*, the攀缘心) that you and all sentient beings now take as your own nature;

second, the originally pure essence of beginningless Bodhi and Nirvana, which is this識精 (shí jīng, the essence of consciousness) that is fundamentally luminous and capable of giving rise to all conditions.
Those who are left behind by conditions do so because sentient beings have abandoned this fundamental luminosity (*mūla-vidyā*).

Although they ultimately proceed together [with it], they fail to realize it and thus wrongly enter the various realms of existence (*gati*). "Billions" (*yi-xia*) refers to the long duration of time through which one cycles;

because there is the rising and sinking of good and evil, it is difficult to find rest. *Kalpa* is a Sanskrit term; its full form is *kalpā*, which here means "division of time. *Wang* (罔) is explained as meaning "non-existent."

In the subsequent section on the establishment of the teachings, it is stated that because sentient beings have sunk into the cycle of birth and death due to afflictions and karma, the Buddha arose out of compassion to establish the teachings for their ultimate deliverance.
As the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng lun) says: "Riding upon the path of reality (*yathābhūta-mārga*), he came to achieve perfect enlightenment.

Because the truth is equal and its essence is free from falsehood, it is called "reality" (*yathābhūta*); this is the True Body (*dharmakāya*). Riding upon and treading this Dharma, he appeared in the world to benefit living beings.
Therefore, it is said that "coming to accomplish" refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body). Regarding the "Gate of Great Compassion" (*mahāmaitrī-mukha*):

"Great" (*mahā*) serves to distinguish it from the "small"; "Compassion" (*maitrī*) is the name for bestowing happiness; and "Gate" (*mukha*) has the meaning of providing passage for sentient beings. The *Daśabhūmivibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"Based on the Gate of Great Compassion, one speaks of the *vinaya* precepts. The *Vinaya-śāstra* states: "Based on the Gate of Great Compassion, [the Buddha] skillfully bestows secret methods. Furthermore, the *Vinaya* says: "The world..."
The World-Honored One, out of compassionate concern for sentient beings, preaches the Dharma to open their minds, just as one opens a gate.

Now, about to set forth my intent: afflictions and delusions are difficult to clear away; they must be removed through skillful means. Therefore, one first establishes the precepts to restrain and admonish against transgressions. Once concentration and wisdom arise, afflictions and delusions are naturally dispelled.
Thus one comes to know that the precepts are the preliminary manifestation of right practice and the vanguard in the destruction of evil; they are that which exhausts the source of suffering.
Liberation from birth and death has suffering, affliction, and delusion as its source; because one destroys these delusions to manifest the principle, it is called "exhaustion. The Vinaya states:

"Within my Dharma, practice the pure conduct (brahmacarya) with joy, exhaust the source of suffering, and eliminate the karma of outflows. This refers to the sevenfold karma of the three poisons, which is termed "karma with outflows" and also "mobile karma.
The activities of body and speech are mobile and thus conflict with the principle; if one does not first prevent delusion...
Following the dust of sensory desires, one now establishes the restraint of the precepts so that karma and delusion have no means of arising; thus the Vinaya states:

"In order to subdue the three poisons and bring them to an end, the training in increased virtue (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*) is ordained. This is illustrated by the following four lines of metaphor: felling the tree corresponds to thoroughly exhausting the source of suffering;

pruning the branches corresponds to first eliminating the seeds and fruits of out-flowing karma (*āsrava*) so they have no basis for existence—meaning that karma does not continue—and the visible roots and stumps gradually wither away.
This means that the three delusions have been eternally extinguished and eliminated; "厥" (jue) serves here as a concluding indicator.
As the *Shijing* says, "He cultivated his virtue," where "致" (zhì) refers to the cause leading to this result; thus, it is explained as "this."

In the first section of the subsequent chapter explaining the composition of this commentary, it states: "The compilation [of the Vinaya] was finalized in the Western Lands (India) more than one thousand years ago;
its translation and transmission to the Eastern Xia (China) have been for nearly four hundred years.

It further clarifies that "Central India" refers to the Middle Land between Heaven and Earth (*zhōng tiān dì zhī zhōng*), and "Brahmāvarta" (*fàntiān*) refers to the descendants of the Brahmā Heaven, namely the Five Regions of India (*wǔ tiānzhū guó*), where three thousand suns and moons shine.
The "Ten Thousand and Two Thousand" refers to the center of the world-system.
The Five Schools—namely, the Mahīśāsaka, Sarvāstivāda, Dharmaguptaka, Kāśyapīya, and Mahāsaṃghika—shared the same teacher as the Saṃmitīya;

they branched out from the fundamental Mahāsaṃghika school. According to their respective inclinations and preferences, they formed distinct schools through their differing tenets, establishing their own traditions.

Regarding the world, it is said that [the Dharma] is vied for and performed; above, it is based on the Central Heaven (Madhyadeśa) where it was practiced side-by-side with other systems, while below, it clarifies its exclusive propagation in the Eastern Land (China).

"Translation" (*yi*) refers to the act of rendering from Sanskrit into Chinese. To say one "translates" means to change the Sanskrit into Chinese. According to the *Zhou Li* (Rites of Zhou), the languages of the four quarters were each managed by their own officials:
those of the East were called *ji*, those of the South *xiang*, those of the West *didi*, and those of the North... [the text here is incomplete].
It is said that "yi" (translation) is based on the fact that Buddhism originated from the West; logically, it should be called *diti*.

However, during the Han dynasty, translators who were frequently engaged in northern trade were also proficient in Western languages. At that time, as the Buddha-dharma came from the West, these translators rendered it into Chinese;
for this reason, Buddhist scriptures are all termed "translations" (*yi*). Furthermore, because of this region, the land of the East is also called "Huaxia," signifying a land of beautiful clothing.

The *Cai Zhang* (Colored Chapters) refers to the *Huà Dàguó* (Flowering Great Country), which is the *Xià* (Xiá). It is divided into four sections, broadly encompassing the five divisions [of Vinaya].

Of these, the first three—the *Jièběn* (Prātimokṣa Sūtra) and the *Guǎnglǜ* (Extensive Vinaya)—have already been translated in this land. The *Gēnběn Shēngqí* (Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya) has also circulated in the Eastern Land (*Dōngxià*).

However, since the beginning of Emperor Ming of the Han’s dream at night and the subsequent transmission of the Dharma by Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna, the foundations were merely being laid; there had not yet been time to establish the complete structure, and the task has spanned the era of the Cáo family.

Two hundred years ago during the Wei dynasty, Dharmakāla established the ten-person ordination based on the *Caturvargika-karman* (Four-Part Vinaya Rite), and he subsequently produced the *Sengqi jixin* (Essentials of the Mahāsāṃghika Precepts) for the assembly to recite and study.
During the Yao Qin period, when the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) was first translated, people immediately relied upon it;
subsequently, the extensive texts of the three schools—the *Caturvargika*, *Mahāsāṃghika*, and *Mahīśāsaka*—were all transmitted to this land.
People said that the *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya] accorded with the textual principles of the original precepts, and thus they abandoned the *Sarvāstivāda* for the extensive *Mahāsāṃghika*.
It was not until the time of Dharma-cōng, the Vinaya Master of the Northern Wei, that he investigated the essence of ordination (*upasampadā*) and finally ceased the use of the *Mahāsāṃghika*.

Regarding the initial transmission of the *Dharmaguptaka*, the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* states: "From the beginning of its introduction, the Vinaya Master named Dharma-cōng transmitted it orally; at that time, the *śramaṇas* who propagated it..."

Subsequently, Yunhui (雲暉), Yuan (願), and others followed in his footsteps to transmit the lamp of the Dharma, each upholding the oral teachings. As listed extensively among the various masters in the subsequent *Chao* (Commentary), their propagation was very numerous;

hence it is said that they "widely propagated" [the teachings]. Alternatively, although the various sections were translated, the four... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)
The *Yeshu* (Outline of the Karmic Causes) states: "When China was unified under one rule, approximately four parts of the text were received and recited;

This is what is meant by "manifesting. Does the Great Sage not already know that person? A single word [of the] *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* is called "skillfully understanding one word," which is termed a *vinaya-dhara* (master of discipline).

As the refuge of humans and devas, they aid the Buddha in propagating his transformation—would it not be most appropriate to call them "Excellent Commentaries"? The *Analects* says: "Suddenly..."

In providing a general account of the methods before the various texts were compiled, I have made deletions and additions according to the circumstances; therefore, I place this preface at the beginning.
This "text" refers to the *Shu-yao*. As the *Analects* says: "When the Master was in peril at Kuang, he said: 'Since King Wen has passed away, does not the cultural heritage (*wen*) reside here?

"If this culture is lost, what can the people of Kuang do for me? [The Master] said: "The transmission covers all beings of the age.

This is the vehicle mounted upon the six *pāramitās*. Because these five operate in unison, they are said to be "yoked side by side. The *Zhuanlun* also states:

"The five vehicles are yoked together on the path of the precepts, and the various sages follow one another along the thoroughfare of practice. The *Jiaochao* says: "They serve as the guide and leader for the five vehicles.
The present text attaches this to the general designation of the seven assemblies (*saptasaṃgha*), namely: bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, [śrāmaṇerī], upāsaka, and upāsikā.

Question: The upper passage states that "the five vehicles were established so that all sentient beings might receive their bounty," while the lower passage states that "the seven assemblies were all moistened by its grace. Since these two textual intentions overlap, how are they to be distinguished? Answer:

The upper passage is based on the original intention of the author of the *Chao* (Commentary), whereas the lower passage is based on the actual benefits obtained by those who encountered the teaching. Reflecting upon this, the distinction will become clear. This concludes the section.

The Sangha assembles according to the required quorum; they receive the *chanda* (consent) and establish the boundaries (*sīmā*). The Sangha’s net of mutual protection—such as between teacher and disciple—is like the protection of the Dharma.
This includes the procedures for receiving precepts, the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, the summer retreat (*varṣā*), and the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*).

Regarding daily life, this refers to matters such as the two robes and the four medicines, which must be handled according to the rules for host and guest, as well as the care of the sick and the rites for the deceased. Generally speaking, these matters are not mutually exclusive; "rites" refers to the essential formal procedures.

This means that regarding the phenomena of things, one horizontally grasps the essential framework; "framework" refers to the ropes of a net, for by grasping the framework, the net itself becomes naturally orderly.

Now, it is said that the array of the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka) is like a vast net; to grasp its great essentials is metaphorically called "grasping the framework. "Essentials" refers to the pivotal points. The *Chao* says:
"If one raises the collar and grasps the framework, the individual hairs and eyes will naturally fall into order. The *Shangshu* says: "Raise the horizontal [lines]."

To grasp the essential pivot of the guiding principles (*kāṅchuō*) is sufficient to perpetuate the world and establish the teaching; this is what is meant. To "exhaustively master the rules and methods" (*guīyóu*)—where "rules and methods" refers to the norms—is as stated in the *Chāo*:
"When mind and objects reflect one another, every movement accords with the rules and methods. In governing the Sangha and protecting the Dharma, it is vital to know the great essentials;

one need only hold the main framework (*tígāng*). Yet, in daily life, one must always abide by the rules and methods. Because these are subtle and hidden, they must be exhaustively mastered; this is what is meant by "reaching down to the lower [levels]."

The preface to the *Shangshu* states: "Successive dynasties have treasured it as a great instruction; because its chapters were formed through deletion and supplementation, it has been revered by both ancient and modern times.
It is specifically designated as 'Great Instruction' (Daxun) to manifest the Sage’s model."

In the first section of the "Preface to the Compilation," the first four lines describe how ancient [explanations] were unreasonable. It states that "the principles (*li*) are profound and abstruse" (*yuan-ao*), where both terms signify depth.

Furthermore, "profound" (*ao*) refers to the inner chamber of a room; Ban Mañjian stated, "To exhaust the inner sanctum (*hu-ao*) of the former sages," with the commentary explaining that "the inner sanctum" (*hu-nei-ao-shi*) refers to the interior chamber.

Scholars of past and present have not even reached the outer fence, let alone the inner sanctum. Regarding the discussion below, it corresponds to the preceding sentence;
since the text is both deep and abstruse, those who find its gate are rare. As for "discussion," the *Analects* states: "As for issuing decrees, Bi Shen..."
In the age of its initial drafting, it was discussed by Shu; the diplomat Ziyu refined it, and Dongli Zipan gave it its final polish.
The *Preface to the Book of Documents* states: "Though one may discuss the ancient archives and classics, few find their way into them. Zigong said: "The walls of Confucius are several *ren* high;
unless one finds the gate and enters, one will not see the beauty of his ancestral temple nor the abundance of his officials."

"Those who find its gate are few. "Few" means rare. "Matters of various kinds arrayed like a forest" refers to the three types of practice (*tri-yoga*) and two types of observance (*dvi-dhāraṇī*) and other matters analyzed within the text.
"Categories of meaning are not uniform, like the myriad phenomena arrayed in a dense forest" is as stated in the *Chao* (Excerpts): "The myriad realms are arrayed in a dense forest;
what matter is not an observance? The *Karmavācanā Preface* states: "In the past, while residing in the various regions of Guanzhong and Fufeng, I composed [this work]."

The *Xingxi Chao* (Abridged Commentary on Monastic Rituals) fully presents the various categories and miscellaneous characteristics; this is it. Regarding the term "driving forth" (*jiashuo*), Yangzi said:
"Is it not as if the Way of Heaven does not reside in Zhongni? Zhongni was one who 'drove forth' [the teachings]. The commentary notes: "'Driving forth' means to transmit.

The materials left behind consist of either the writings and records of former virtuous masters that have circulated as chapters and notes, or those transmitted orally through successive teaching;

having heard or seen these, I have selected the excellent among them to compile into a work expressed in ink and brush. Thus it is said, "exhausting all that has been seen and heard," where "exhausting" (qìng) means to leave nothing remaining.
In the section "Establishing the Title" within the middle volume, the first two lines describe the act of establishing the title;

Therefore, it says, "the entire work is unified under... "Unified" (*tǒng*) means to converge; that is, all things converge and return to nothing other than these three types of conduct.

The phrase "next, the function is shown" refers to the current *Chao* (Commentary). The sun, moon, and stars are the patterns (*wen*) of Heaven;

the Odes, History, Rites, and Music are the patterns of humanity. As the *Yi Jing* says: "Observe the patterns of Heaven to examine the changes of the seasons; observe the patterns of humanity to transform and perfect the world.
Now, the establishment of this *Chao* by our school’s Vinaya masters is like the existence of the *Wenyan* (Explanatory Words) in the *Yi Jing*. This is the Dharma.
Question: Regarding these characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*), to which category do they belong? Answer: They belong to the category of dharmic characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*).
This is because the textual analysis explains that their characteristics are manifested according to specific matters.

To know lightness and weight means to use the measures of the *dou* and the scales. By using these, one knows increase and decrease;

once they have been analyzed and explained, and then weighed and measured, they become clear and plain, ready to be put into practice. Furthermore, the first two lines belong to the category of teaching (*śāsana*), which corresponds to the character "self-benefit" (*zili*);
the latter two lines belong to the category of practice (*pratipatti*), which corresponds to the character "benefiting others" (*lita*).
This concludes the preceding section; "Teaching and Practice" refers to the eyes and feet respectively. "Deepening one's resources at the pool" means that one can reach the destination;

"discussing self and others" means that both oneself and others are brought to salvation. This "Great Practice" is what the *Heart Sūtra* calls "benefiting oneself and benefiting others," wherein all dharmas are fully complete.

As for the title of this work, it is a record; the meaning of the "Section on Sustaining Practice" (*Zichi bu*) is precisely the commentary (*chao*) that elucidates ritual practice, as observed by the Master Zhiyi in his records.
The title itself clarifies the purport of this entire commentary before one’s eyes.

In describing my own intentions and expressing my thoughts, "thorough and vast" (*zhōngtōng hóngguǎng*) refers to its breadth and magnitude; "scanty and vulgar" (*guālòu*) refers to being isolated, limited, and lacking in learning.

The following metaphors illustrate the two preceding phrases. These originate from Dongfang Shuo’s *Reply to the Guest’s Difficulty*, which states: "To peer at the heavens through a tube; to [measure the ocean] with a conch-shell ladle..."
To measure the ocean with a chopstick or strike a bell—is this capable of penetrating its systematic structure, examining its patterns and principles, or eliciting its sounds?
A *lí* is a type of crab; to measure the ocean with a crab, how could one fathom its depth? The latter two lines are from Zhu Fu’s letter to Zhang Chong, which says:
"It is like a person on the banks of the Yellow River holding a handful of earth to block Mengjin—it is clearly seen [to be futile]."

From this one can infer that the author of this record, though wielding his brush, did not boast of himself. Observe his writings today:
what was unheard of in previous generations, he now refutes the hundred schools and surpasses all other doctrines. When explaining meanings, they are like ice melting and spring water gushing forth.

Because one thinks and perceives without restraint, this constitutes a violation of the precepts; thus the text says, "committed through mental intention. Furthermore, the *Yejieshu* states:

"Regarding all matters of formal adjudication and inquiries concerning the mind, they differ from that school [the Sarvāstivāda]. In that school, the seven branches of body and speech are all within the category of form (*rūpa*), and thus possess the quality of either benefit or harm.

Therefore, the name [of these offenses] is concluded here. Within the Threefold Perfect Teaching (*tricakravāda*), the preceding [categories] belong to the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), whereas this is the Great [Vehicle].

To use the great to resolve the small without waiting for the reception of the great is the meaning of the Perfect and Sudden (yuan-dun). The previous two [teachings] were partial, with an uneven distribution of emptiness and existence;

now, one awakens to the fact that while the provisional teachings differ in name, their essence is one—this applies to both form and non-form alike—and this is the meaning of perfect fusion (yuan-rong).
Having previously followed the provisional to respond to beings for a single period, this now establishes the reality and ultimately reveals it.

It is the meaning of perfection (*pūrṇa*). Furthermore, it is the meaning of perfect wondrousness (*pariniṣpanna*), for the three clusters (*triskandha*) are fused and integrated beyond the reach of conceptual thought.
Moreover, it is the meaning of perfect endowment, for the three vows, the three clusters, the three liberations (*vimokṣa*), and the three bodies (*trikāya*) each mutually possess one another.

That which is called "perfect" refers to the perfect vow, the perfect cluster, the perfect aspiration, the perfect cultivation, the perfect virtue, the perfect realization, the perfect entry into liberation, and the perfect establishment of all sentient beings.
All Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras that teach the Buddha’s realm as not shared with the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) belong to this teaching.
Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* speaks of opening, showing, awakening, and entering; the *Avataṃsaka* speaks of attaining realization immediately upon generating the bodhicitta;

the *Vimalakīrti* speaks of not smelling other fragrances within the campaka grove, such that those who enter this chamber smell only the fragrance of the merits of all Buddhas; and the *Prajñāpāramitā* elucidates the Supreme Vehicle (*agrayāna*).

Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states that there are five practices for one-pointed concentration. Another sutra says: suppose a person enters the great ocean to bathe and then uses the waters of all rivers;
even if the Dragon King Sāgara pours down rain as thick as chariot axles, only the great ocean can receive it, while other lands cannot endure it.
Again, if ten thousand kinds of incense are ground into pills, burning even a single grain suffices to provide the full array of fragrances. Furthermore, the *Lotus Sūtra* speaks of the dew.
The "earth," the "white ox," "nirvāṇa," and the "fat grass of the Snowy Mountains"—categories such as these collectively constitute the basis for the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
Although it is said that the three schools lack principle and are biased and restrictive, since they are separately designated, their underlying intent is not absent.

Because the two preceding systems each have their own adherents, this [Perfect Teaching] directly employs the perfect meaning of the Mahāyāna to resolve the substance of the former; therefore, it merely designates the teaching, which here refers to the teaching-as-indication.
"School" (*zong*) here refers specifically to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) as a single school; it does not mean a partisan faction.

Immediately below, the text correctly demonstrates the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*’s "opening and uniting" [of teachings], which contains two intentions: first, to fully discourse on Buddha-nature for those who are not yet mature, so that they may possess true permanence;

second, to prevent those of dull faculties in the final age from giving rise to views of annihilationism within the Buddha-dharma, thereby averting injury to their wisdom-life and preventing its loss.
Because the Dharma-body is profound, it upholds the precepts so that all may ultimately return to the eternal;
thus the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that those of the two vehicles will ultimately return to nirvāṇa in the future, like flowing water returning to the sea.

Furthermore, the *Lotus Sūtra* states that within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions there is only the One Vehicle—neither two nor three—which expresses the intent of opening and merging [the provisional with the real]. Prior to these two sutras, [the teachings were] expedient.

In truth, they are not the same; there is a vast disparity between them, like that between a large and a small vessel. As for the *Avataṃsaka*, the "large" does not admit the "small," and although the "small" may be present in the assembly, they are as if deaf or mute.

Thus, the Buddha’s capacity to guide sentient beings is not fully exhausted nor is his intent fully realized. When the Tathāgata appeared in the world, it was his original intention to arrive at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* assembly and return to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
As the sutra says: "Within the single Buddha-vehicle, he distinguishes and teaches three"—this is the establishment of provisional means based upon the ultimate reality. Furthermore, it says:
"Opening the gate of expedient means and revealing the true aspect" refers to opening up the provisional to manifest the real.

"Directly abandoning expedient means and teaching only the unsurpassed path" refers to discarding the provisional to establish the real. Thus we know that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* opens the way for śrāvakas to become Buddhas, while the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* supports the minor vehicles and their precepts to discuss the eternal.
Apart from these two sutras, no other scripture possesses this meaning. Ji says: "Tong says that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* [is the one that does]."

The general purport of the teachings of the two sections of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is to cause those of the Two Vehicles to abandon the provisional and enter the real, thereby accomplishing the true gate of the single reality of the Dharma-realm;
all other teachings are merely expedient means. Question: Since both sūtras are alike in opening and harmonizing [the teachings], why is only the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* singled out here?
Answer: Regarding its timing, flavor, and essence, it is the same as the *Lotus Sūtra*; however, it specifically upholds the Vinaya while expounding the Dharma.

Because they are constantly in accord with the ultimate meaning, the principle that the latter subsumes the former is inherently sufficient. Regarding the definitive understanding of the provisional vehicle (*upāya-yāna*):

the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that the definitive teaching on the *śrāvaka* dharma is the king of all sūtras. Furthermore, the Patriarch [Huiyuan] stated: "Nirvāṇa is the ultimate exhaustion of the provisional teachings;

it is the definitive understanding of the true meaning. "Provisional" (*quán*) refers to expedient strategies used temporarily which are subsequently discarded; "real" (*shí*) refers to the authentic record that is ultimately realized.

Since all that precedes the two sutras cited as the ultimate goal (*zhǐguī*) is provisional teaching, the following section correctly demonstrates the truth. The two preceding lines clarify the essence:

regarding the perfuming of seeds within the *ālayavijñāna*, the Commentary states, "Perfuming the fundamental *ālaya* consciousness forms virtuous seeds," and further states, "Not falsely taking objects as conditions, there is only the single consciousness which, through transformation according to conditions, manifests both 'that' and 'this. To comprehend deluded feelings, one must know deluded karma."

Therefore, when one performs the ritual of formal reception, it perfumes the deluded mind within the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), forming seeds of goodness; this is the essence of the precepts (*śīla*).
Because these fundamental seeds perfume the mind, they possess constant power to draw forth subsequent practice and initiate functional activity.

Thus, regarding all objects of transgression, one is able to remember, maintain, and prevent them; as the mind moves and acts, this [precept] in turn perfumes the storehouse consciousness. Question: How many types of perfuming are there?

The answer is: First, the initial undertaking of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) perfumes and produces the *avijñapti* (unmanifest); second, the *avijñapti* then perfumes and produces the subsequent practice;

third, within that practice, both *vijñapti* and *avijñapti* perfume and revert to the original undertaking. If one discusses the locus of this perfuming, it permeates the mind and consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*).

Question: According to the *Awakening of Faith*, there are two types of perfuming—internal and external. To which of these does this belong? Answer: That treatise takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as the internal perfuming factor.

The teachings of the Dharma-friends serve as external perfuming (*bāhya-vāsana*), while now, taking the fundamental reality of the single consciousness (*eka-vijñāna*) as internal perfuming (*antara-vāsana*), one forms both the unconditioned precepts (*anabhisaṃskāra-śīla*) and the external perfuming;

this is the seed of the roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla-bīja*). "Good" is used to distinguish it from evil. It is named after its analogy: just as worldly grains and fruits all possess seeds, the name "seed" has a general meaning that requires careful discernment.

First, regarding the ten realms (*daśa-dhātu*), starting with the four miserable destinies (*catur-gati*): [The text continues with a detailed analysis of the nature of seeds across the various realms, distinguishing between those that are inherently good, evil, or indeterminate, and how they function through internal and external perfuming.]

Of the remaining six [faculties], those that perform evil are unwholesome, while the others are wholesome. Next, among the wholesome, there are the out-flowing (sāsrava) seeds of humans and devas, and the non-out-flowing (anāsrava) seeds of the four noble ones.
Within the noble ones, the three vehicles are partial and provisional, whereas only the Buddha is complete and real. Now, this text concerning the seeds of the precepts merely excludes what is evil;
yet, in relation to humans and devas, these are non-out-flowing seeds, and in relation to the partial and provisional, they are the seeds of the complete and real. Thus it is for the practitioner.

One should know that the essence originally received is itself the single essence, the seed-dharma of the three Buddhas. As the *Lotus Sūtra* states, "The Buddha-seed arises from conditions"—this is precisely that meaning.

Following this, the three clusters (*tri-skandha*) of practice are shown: namely, the cluster of restraining discipline (*saṃvara-śīla*), the cluster of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the cluster of benefiting sentient beings (*sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla*).
Whenever one precept is cited, all three clusters are fully present; likewise, whenever one cluster is cited, the others are mutually complete. Thus it should be known.

Initially receiving the Perfect [Teaching], one gives rise to the three vows; in accordance with these, one reverently maintains them; through the Perfect cultivation of the three practices, one achieves the cause and evokes the fruit;

and one perfectly realizes the three bodies. The three vows are precisely the three aggregates (triskandha) and the three bodies; the three aggregates are also precisely the three bodies and the three vows; the three bodies are also precisely the three vows and the three aggregates.
When mind and Buddha are without difference and cause and effect are non-dual—one who can act in this manner is only then called [a true practitioner].
The perfect precepts (*pariśuddha-śīla*) are the *pāramitā*, which is ultimate liberation (*vimukti*). "Slight indulgence" refers to a momentary lapse; the Commentary states:
"If one does not exert diligent self-restraint and slightly indulges the deluded mind, it will again permeate the fundamental delusion, increasing its depth and gravity until it forms karmic conduct.

This is the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Mahāyāna, such as the prohibitions against stinginess and anger in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* recounts the sound of a bracelet.

The mind that discriminates between male and female forms defiles the precepts; this concludes the section on names. Since the capacities of sentient beings vary in depth, the teachings are divided into beginning and end.

Although what preceded was "Great," it did not yet reach the ultimate source of transformation; only upon arriving at the *Nirvāṇa* Sūtra is it called the "definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*). Therefore, it is termed the "ultimate culmination of the Mahāyāna teachings."

In the *Huizong*, the first two lines above establish the profound [principle], while the subsequent section synthesizes and unifies the ten recitations (*śāriputra-vinaya*). Taking form (*rūpa*) as the essence of the precepts (*śīla-sarīra*) merely prevents the seven branches [of misconduct];

The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "This person has extensively examined the three capacities and closely scrutinized the two canons;

To relinquish material wealth is not what is emphasized; it is knowing that the mind is empty and pervasive. That sensory objects are not the fundamental roots is to understand the definitive meaning of consciousness.
Briefly citing these as proof, they entirely differ from the "Small Vehicle" (Hīnayāna). In summary, the correspondence with the preceding section can be understood. How magnificent!

Master Nanshan, by means of the two teachings and three schools, judged and explained the temporal teachings of one lifetime transmitted to the East, aligning them with the four teachings of Tiantai and the ten schools of Xuanzang.

To insult the Sages brings retribution that is not light; therefore, exert yourselves! Exert yourselves!
